t.late baroque towns of the val di noto@36:
On 11 January 1693, a catastrophic earthquake struck southeastern Sicily, destroying dozens of towns and killing tens of thousands of people. What happened next is one of the great chapters in the history of town planning. Noto, which stood on a hill some kilometres away, was abandoned, and a new town was built from scratch on a gentler slope, with a grid of streets, grand stairways, churches and palaces, all in the soft, honey-coloured local limestone that glows gold and pink at sunset. Together with seven other towns rebuilt after the earthquake, including Ragusa, Modica and Scicli, Noto was listed by UNESCO in 2002 as the Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto.

The main street, the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, runs through the town past the cathedral, which partially collapsed in 1996 and was painstakingly restored, reopening in 2007. Around it, palaces with extravagant balconies held up by carved monsters, horses and cherubs line the side streets; the balconies of the Palazzo Nicolaci on Via Corrado Nicolaci are especially wild. In May, the Infiorata festival covers that street with intricate designs made of flower petals. Wandering at dusk, when the stone glows and the evening passeggiata fills the streets, is one of the great pleasures of Sicily.

The food deserves its fame. Noto is known for its granita, especially almond, and for its pastry shops, where you can have a granita with a brioche for breakfast, as Sicilians do on summer mornings.

The surrounding countryside is a landscape of almond and olive groves, carob trees and dry-stone walls, crossed by deep limestone gorges, the cave, with ancient tombs cut into their walls. The roads between Noto, Palazzolo Acreide and Ragusa wind through this landscape with long, flowing bends and little traffic. To the south, the coast has beautiful beaches and the Vendicari nature reserve, a coastal wetland where flamingos winter. The roads can be patched and potholed, and in summer the heat is fierce, so ride early in the day.

Noto has fuel, garages, hotels and restaurants. Avola, a few kilometres away, gives its name to Nero d'Avola, the grape behind Sicily's best-known red wine; try a glass with dinner, not before the ride.
t.old town of corfu@39.6,19.9:
Corfu is where the Greek world met Venice, and the old town shows it in every lane. For more than four centuries, from the late fourteenth century to the end of the eighteenth, the island belonged to the Venetian Republic, which fortified it against the Ottomans, so the town has two great fortresses, tall narrow houses with washing lines, and a maze of alleys called kantounia, which are cooler and more intimate than any grand boulevard. UNESCO listed the old town in 2007. The French arrived briefly under Napoleon and left the Liston, an arcade modelled on Paris's Rue de Rivoli, and the British, who ruled the islands from 1815 to 1864, left cricket, which is still played on the Spianada, the broad green esplanade by the sea, and ginger beer, called tsitsibira.

The town is a living place, not a museum, with a daily market, small churches where the bells ring on the hour and a lively evening scene around the Liston. Regional food is distinctive, with pastitsada, a spiced beef and pasta dish, sofrito, veal in a garlic and vinegar sauce, and kumquat liqueur from the island's orchards. Mix a little of each into your day.

Corfu town has about twenty-seven thousand people, so fuel, parking and services are easy. The old town itself is a maze that you walk, and the busy road along the harbour is crowded in summer. Ferries run from Igoumenitsa on the mainland and from Italian ports, and day boats cross to Saranda in Albania, making a link with the other half of this ride.

The island is far better ridden outside July and August, when the roads are crowded with rental scooters. The north has a high, wooded spine with the mountain of Pantokrator rising to over nine hundred metres, with narrow, twisty roads, olive groves and abandoned villages like Old Perithia, and the coves of the west are reached by steep lanes. Surfaces are patchy, with loose gravel on corners and sudden potholes. Spring brings wildflowers, and autumn sea warm enough for a swim, and the island is green because it rains in winter.
t.birka and hovgarden@59.3,17.5:
Before Stockholm existed, there was Birka. In the eighth century, on a small island called Bjorko in Lake Malaren, a few kilometres west of the modern city, traders and craftsmen set up a market town, and for about two hundred years it was the most important trading centre in Sweden. Merchants brought furs, iron and slaves, and carried back silver, glass, silk and spices. Coins from Arabia and swords from the Rhineland have turned up in the graves, and a Christian missionary, Ansgar, came here around 830 to preach, with limited success. By the end of the tenth century the town had been abandoned, perhaps because the lake had become too shallow for ships as the land slowly rose after the ice age.

Across the water, on the neighbouring island of Adelso, lies Hovgarden, the royal estate that governed Birka. The huge mounds on the shore, the Kungshogarna, are burial places of local rulers, and the stone church, built in the twelfth century, stands next to a runestone. Together the two sites were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1993 as an example of a Viking Age trading settlement and its administrative centre.

The island of Birka is reached by boat from Stockholm in summer, so a rider cannot simply roll up on a bike. The ride is to the lake itself, and to Adelso, which can be reached by a small, free road ferry from the island of Munso. Beyond that, you walk. The road out of Stockholm crosses the Drottningholm bridge and runs along quiet lanes among the farms and villages of the island of Ekero, with views over the water and the royal palace of Drottningholm on the way. The speed limits are firmly policed and traffic is light outside summer weekends.

Ekero has about eleven thousand people, with fuel and shops, and Stenhamra, a smaller place, has some services. The best seasons are late May to September, when the days are long and the light stays for hours. Pack insect repellent for the woods and a picnic, since cafes are few, and bring a jacket for the breeze on the water. The Birka museum, with its model of the Viking town, is worth a visit before you walk the ramparts.
t.skogskyrkogarden@59.3,18.1:
The best cemetery in the world is not a bad claim to make for a forest on the southern edge of Stockholm. Skogskyrkogarden, the Woodland Cemetery, was designed by two young architects, Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, who won a competition in 1915 with a plan that used the existing pine forest and a gravel pit as the starting point. They built it in stages over the next twenty-five years, and it was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1994 as a masterpiece of twentieth-century landscape design. The idea was that death should not be shown as a dark hole, but as a return to nature.

You enter along a long straight path, with a stone cross standing alone against the sky, and gradually the forest opens out. The first thing you see is a gentle grassy hill, a man-made mound with a ring of elm trees at the top, called the Meditation Grove. Graves lie scattered in the forest, unhedged, with simple markers under the pines, so that families can mourn without feeling shut in. The Woodland Chapel, the first building Asplund completed here, has a steep roof of black shingles and a portico of slender white columns, a quiet, almost childlike design, that feels like a small house in the woods. Nearby, Lewerentz's chapels of Faith, Hope and the Holy Cross have a more severe, classical air. Greta Garbo is buried here, in a quiet corner, and the visit is a favourite for architects and walkers.

Getting here is easy. It lies in the district of Enskede, south of the city centre, with the metro station of Skogskyrkogarden on the green line, and a main road passing nearby. For a rider it is a short, simple run from the centre, through typical Stockholm suburbs, with good roads, tram lines and many cyclists. Speed cameras and limits are strictly observed, and parking near the entrance is free. Fuel and food are plentiful in the city, and the neighbourhoods of Arsta and Sodermalm have cafes and shops.

Autumn is when the cemetery is most beautiful, with the leaves turning gold and the light low. In winter, with snow on the ground and a few candles at the graves, it has a solemn, magical atmosphere. Walk slowly, speak quietly, and remember that this is a working cemetery.
t.noto@36.9,15.1:
Noto died on the evening of 11 January 1693 and was reborn on another hill. An earthquake that struck south-east Sicily that night destroyed dozens of towns, and killed tens of thousands of people. The survivors of Noto decided to abandon the old site, high on a mountain, and build a new town a few kilometres south, on a gentle slope nearer the sea. The result is a baroque city planned on a grid, with long streets, broad stairs and a succession of churches and palaces, all made of soft honey-coloured limestone that turns gold at sunset. The late baroque towns of the Val di Noto are listed by UNESCO, and Noto is the star.

The main street, Corso Vittorio Emanuele, runs through three squares with a cathedral and a town hall, and the stairs up to the cathedral make a stage for the whole town. The dome of the cathedral collapsed in 1996, after a long period of neglect, and was rebuilt and reopened in 2007. The Via Nicolaci, with its wrought-iron balconies held up by stone sphinxes and grotesques, is carpeted in flowers every May for the Infiorata, a festival that draws crowds.

Noto is also the centre of a food culture. Almonds grown in the surrounding fields go into granita and marzipan, and the sweet shops sell a wide range. Avola, nearby, gave its name to the Nero d'Avola grape, which makes a rich red wine. The Vendicari nature reserve, on the coast to the south, is a place of salt pans, beaches and watchtowers where flamingos stop in migration.

The riding is easy and open. Roads cross a landscape of dry-stone walls, carob and olive trees, with long views to the sea. Surfaces can be rough, with potholes and cobbles in the old towns, and the heat in summer is intense. The main roads are fast, with trucks. Expect narrow streets and one-way systems in the old town, and park outside the centre. Noto has eighteen thousand people and fuel stations on the approach roads. Avola, with twenty-nine thousand, has more.

Spring and autumn are best. Winter is mild, and the baroque stone looks warm in low light. In midsummer the stone reflects the heat.
t.windhoek@-22.6,17.1:
Windhoek sits at about 1,700 metres in the middle of Namibia, in a bowl of hills that gives it a cooler, drier climate than most of the country. It is the capital and by far the largest city, with a population approaching three hundred thousand, and a mix of German colonial buildings, modern shopping centres and sprawling townships. The Christuskirche, a Lutheran church with a pale stone facade, stands on a hill in the middle of the town and has become the city's best-known landmark.

Namibia was a German colony until the First World War, and the legacy shows in the architecture, the bakeries, the beer and a language still spoken in some quarters. Beer is a good example: the country brews under the old German purity law, and a cold lager at a terrace in the evening is a fine end to a day. Game meat, from kudu to oryx and springbok, appears on menus alongside the sausages and schnitzel, and biltong, the air-dried meat, is sold everywhere.

The road to Windhoek from the Gamsberg and Kuiseb passes is a ride across the edge of the Namib. The Gamsberg Pass drops from the highlands toward the desert, with long views over a landscape of red rock and pale grass, and the surface is a mix of gravel and tarmac. Gravel here can be loose, corrugated and deep in places, so ride within your limits and keep your speed down. Wildlife, from kudu to baboons, can step onto the road, and long distances between towns mean a breakdown is a serious matter.

Windhoek has everything: fuel, repairs, supermarkets and hotels, and it is the place to stock up before any long ride. Beyond the city, stations can be hundreds of kilometres apart, and you should fill at every chance, carry water and tell someone your route. Cell coverage is patchy outside the towns.

The dry season, roughly May to October, is the best time to ride, with clear skies and cool mornings, though nights can be near freezing at altitude. Summer brings heat and occasional thunderstorms. The sky at night, far from city lights, is spectacular.
t.pollinello@39.9,16.2:
Pollinello is a small spot of Calabrian hill country with no big name attached, and its real importance is where it sits: a few kilometres from the foot of the Pollino massif, in the north of the region, close to the border with Basilicata. Do not look for a pass or a monument. Think of it as a doorway into the Pollino National Park, the largest protected area in Italy, with Morano Calabro and the town of Castrovillari as the places that organise daily life around it.

The park is wild country. Pollino is famous for the Bosnian pine, the loricato, a twisted, ancient tree that clings to bare limestone ridges high above the valleys, some individuals said to be centuries old. Wolves live in these woods, along with roe deer and golden eagles. The roads that climb toward the massif from Morano, a hill town built in a steep cone like a nativity scene, are narrow and quiet, with sharp hairpins, patchy asphalt and the odd stray cow on the road.

Castrovillari, with about twenty thousand people, is the sensible place for fuel, supermarkets and a proper lunch, and Morano is smaller, at around three thousand. Frascineto, close by, is an Arbëreshë village, a community of Albanian speakers who settled in southern Italy after the Ottoman conquests of the fifteenth century and who kept their language and a Greek Orthodox rite in a Catholic country. That kind of layering is typical of Calabria, a region settled and resettled many times over.

Be honest about the weather: up high, snow can close the smaller roads from late autumn until spring, and summer afternoons bring storms that crack over the ridges. Morning is best, when the air is cool and the shepherds' dogs are quiet. Fill up in town before you head into the hills, since stations are thin once you leave the main roads, and carry water. The massif rewards the effort with space, silence and, on a clear day, the Ionian Sea hazy beyond the plain.
t.valle infernale@38.1,16.0:
Valle Infernale is a name that makes a rider sit up, and Aspromonte, the mountain mass of Calabria's far south, does live up to it in its way. The nearest villages are small: Africo Vecchio, a few kilometres away, and Bovalino Superiore, a hill town above the coastal town of Bovalino.

Africo Vecchio is a ghost town, and its story explains a lot about Calabria. The old village clung to a ridge in the mountains, poor and isolated, and after floods in October 1951 the people were moved down to the coast and the old houses were abandoned. Walking among the roofless buildings is sobering. In this region many mountain villages emptied this way, and the silence they left is part of what makes the landscape feel so strange and so untouched.

The riding is tough and rewarding. Roads here are narrow, steep and often neglected, with landslides, rock fall and gravel in the bends, so keep speed honest and expect no help nearby. Mobile coverage fades, and a breakdown means a long walk. In return you get tall beech and fir woods, the huge boulders of the rocky valleys, eagle country and long views down to the sea, with Sicily and sometimes Etna visible on a clear day. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, because summer heat is heavy and winter brings snow at altitude.

Fuel is the main practical point. There are no stations in the mountains, so fill up on the coast, at Bovalino or along the SS106, the busy Ionian road, before climbing. Bovalino Superiore has a bar or two and a little life, but do not rely on a hot meal at every turn. Bring water and a spare layer, and tell someone your route. It is the kind of place that makes you grateful for a working engine.
t.sesriem junction@-24.5,15.8:
Sesriem is the gate to the dunes. The word means six straps in Afrikaans, and the name comes from the early settlers, who tied six leather thongs together to lower a bucket into the narrow canyon here, which holds water long after the rains. The junction sits at the entrance to the Namib-Naukluft Park, in the heart of the Namib desert, and from it a tarred road runs sixty kilometres to Sossusvlei, a white clay pan surrounded by some of the tallest dunes in the world, which rise to around three hundred metres and glow orange and red at sunrise.

The riding here is a mix of gravel and sand. The roads in the surrounding country, including the D707, are mostly gravel, with corrugations, soft patches and occasional rocky sections, and they cross wide plains of pale grass, with the red dunes on one side and rocky mountains on the other. Wind blows hard, especially in the afternoon, and dust can reduce visibility. In the early morning and evening, the light is magnificent, and the shadows on the dunes are sharp. Temperatures vary widely, from cool, even cold, nights to hot days, and rain, though rare, can flood the dry riverbeds.

The park gates open at sunrise and close at sunset, so those who want to see the dunes at first light need to stay in the campsite inside the gate, and a fee is charged at the entrance. The final stretch to Sossusvlei is deep sand, and most visitors leave their vehicle at a car park and take a shuttle. Sesriem Canyon, a narrow gorge about thirty metres deep, is a short walk from the entrance, and offers shade. Dune 45, beside the road, is easy to climb, though the sand is heavy.

Fuel is available at Sesriem, but supplies can be limited, so arrive with a full tank, and carry more if you plan to explore the gravel roads. Solitaire, about eighty kilometres north, has a petrol station, a small shop and a bakery famous for its apple pie. Carry plenty of water, since the desert is dry and the sun is strong.

Stay for sunset if you can. The shadows climbing the dunes are a lasting memory.
t.kalmar@56.7,16.4:
Kalmar has been guarding the south-eastern coast of Sweden for eight hundred years, and the castle shows it. Kalmar Castle, a Renaissance palace with moat, towers and green copper roofs, sits on a small island at the edge of town, rebuilt in the sixteenth century by the Vasa kings from a medieval fortress. In 1397 a treaty was signed here that united Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown in the Kalmar Union, which lasted, on and off, for over a century, and the town still carries that history proudly.

The old town is a mix of grid-pattern streets and pastel wooden houses, with a cathedral in baroque style and a harbor. Kalmar was also the departure point for the Kalmar Nyckel, the ship that carried the first Swedish settlers to the Delaware River in 1638, to found New Sweden. The Kalmar Strait, between the mainland and the long island of Öland, is shallow and sheltered, and is the setting for the town's life.

For riders, Kalmar is the gateway to Öland. The Öland Bridge, about six kilometers long, opened in 1972 and for a time was the longest bridge in Europe, and it arcs high above the strait, with big views from the crest. On the island, the main road runs along the length of a flat limestone plateau called the alvar, a barren, windswept landscape of thin grass, wildflowers and stone walls, studded with old windmills. Borgholm, with its ruined castle, and the Iron Age fort at Eketorp are among the stops. Wind is the main hazard, as gusts on the bridge and the open plateau can push a bike about.

Kalmar has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and it is the logical place to prepare for the island. Färjestaden, on the island side of the bridge, is also well served. The best months are June to August, with warm days and long light, though the island is busy in July. Spring brings orchids on the alvar, and autumn has bird migration. Winter is cold and windy, and the bridge can close in storms. Speed cameras and limits are enforced, and elk and deer are a hazard on the mainland.
t.nicolosi@37.6,15.0:
Nicolosi is the town where Etna starts to feel real. It sits on the southern slope of the volcano at around seven hundred metres, a place of low houses built from black lava stone, steep streets and a surprising number of cafes, and it is the usual gateway for anyone heading up the mountain. Above it, the dark cones of Monti Rossi, formed in the eruption of 1669, look like two big red-brown humps against the sky. That eruption was one of the most destructive in the volcano's history, and its lava flowed down the slopes and reached the walls of Catania, leaving a landscape that still looks raw.

Etna is the tallest active volcano in Europe, at a little over three thousand three hundred metres, though the exact height changes with each eruption, and the whole mountain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The soil from its ash is fertile, and on the lower slopes you find vineyards, pistachio and citrus orchards, and fields of prickly pear. The wine made here is highly regarded, and a glass of local red with a plate of pasta is a good reward after a day on the bike.

For riders, Nicolosi is the base and the starting line. The road from here to Rifugio Sapienza, the provincial road that climbs the south flank, is wide and well surfaced, with a series of bends through lava fields and pine woods. The gradient is steady, and the views of the sea and Catania open behind you as you climb. Be careful of ash and grit on the surface after eruptions, and of cold, fast-changing weather higher up. Traffic can be heavy at weekends and in summer, when buses and tour groups go up and down.

The town has everything you might need, from fuel to supermarkets, pharmacies and restaurants. Fill the tank here before the climb, as there is nothing above except the souvenir shops and cafes around the refuge. There are good bakeries too, and the Sicilian morning ritual of a brioche stuffed with granita is worth trying. Catania, about twenty kilometres south, is the nearest large city with an airport and plenty of services.

Nicolosi also has the Etna park office, where you can find maps and information on the trails, the cable car and local guides. Check conditions before going up, because the authorities close access to the upper slopes when the volcano is active, and it is worth listening to what they say.
t.rifugio sapienza@37.7,15.0:
Rifugio Sapienza is the end of the road for most visitors to Etna, and the place where the volcano turns from background into foreground. At around nineteen hundred metres on the southern flank, it is a cluster of buildings, a cable car station, souvenir stalls and bars in a landscape of black cinder and lava. The air is thin and cold, even in July, and the ground is crunchy underfoot. Nearby are the Silvestri craters, which formed in 1886 and can be walked around in a short loop, giving a close look at the colour of the rocks and the steam rising from cracks.

The road to get here is the best part. Climbing from Nicolosi, it winds up through pine and broom into barren lava flows, past old eruption fronts that cut across the slope like frozen rivers. The bends are generous, the tarmac is decent, and the views over Catania and the Ionian Sea are large and blue. The recent lava fields flank the road in places and are jet black, with little vegetation. Be aware that eruptions can cover the road with ash and fine grit, and that the surface is sometimes damaged by lava flows or frost.

The cable car runs from here to roughly twenty-five hundred metres, and from there guided tours go on to the higher craters, depending on the volcano's mood. Heights that were once reachable can be closed at short notice, so ask at the station. Wear warm clothes. The wind can be fierce, and you will notice the temperature drop at once when you get off the bike.

The bars and restaurants serve coffee, sandwiches, hot food and regional specialities, and prices are high because everything is carried up the mountain. It is worth buying a hot drink and taking it outside to look at the moonscape.

In winter, the area is a small ski resort, and the road may be closed or require chains. In summer, the weather is usually dry, but fog and thunderstorms can arrive without warning. Mornings are the best time for clear views and quiet roads.
t.zafferana etnea@37.7,15.1:
Zafferana Etnea sits on the eastern side of Etna, a town of about nine thousand people stretched along a ridge above the sea, and it has a reputation that is half sweet and half dangerous. The sweet half is honey. The slopes around the town are rich in flowering plants, from broom and wild thyme to orange blossom, and the honey made here is some of the best in Sicily, with a festival in autumn that fills the main street with stalls. The dangerous half is the volcano. In 1992 a lava flow from Etna advanced towards the town, and engineers and the army worked for months to divert it, with helicopters dropping concrete blocks and explosives breaking up the lava tubes. The flow stopped just short of the houses, and the story is still told with a mixture of pride and relief.

The ride here from the coast, or from the ring road around the volcano, is a pleasant one. The roads are narrow and winding, bordered by stone walls, citrus groves and vineyards, with the black volcanic soil showing between the rows. The surface is generally decent but varies, and some corners are tight enough to need a low gear. Etna is always there above you, usually with a thread of steam from the summit. Traffic is lighter than on the south side, and the town is much less crowded with tour groups.

Zafferana has the full range of services. There are petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, and the town square is a good place for coffee and a pastry. Local specialities include almond sweets, chestnut dishes in autumn, and wines from the slopes of Etna. The nearby town of Santa Venerina is part of the same pleasant, lived-in landscape, and the coast, with its sea cliffs and fishing villages, is a short ride away.

The best months to come are late spring and early autumn, when the air is clear and warm but not hot, and the vegetation is at its most colourful. In summer the lower slopes can be very hot, and in winter the upper road can be icy or closed.

If you have time, ask for directions to the viewpoints that look into the Valle del Bove, the great crater-like depression on Etna's eastern side. It is a vast, strange place, and a reminder of the scale of what lives next door.
t.taormina@37.9,15.3:
Taormina clings to a terrace of Monte Tauro on the east coast of Sicily, about two hundred metres above the sea, and from almost every street you look straight out across the Ionian to the coast of Calabria. Mount Etna stands to the south, smoking above the haze, and on a clear day the whole thing looks painted. Giardini-Naxos lies below by the water, and the little hilltop village of Castelmola sits above the town, a short, tight climb of a kilometre or so that is well worth the effort for the view.

The town's centrepiece is the ancient Greek theatre, built in the third century BC and rebuilt by the Romans. It is cut into the hillside, and the stage frames Etna in a way that no designer could improve. Taormina has long been a favourite of travellers: Goethe wrote about it, D. H. Lawrence lived here for a time, and in the nineteenth century it became a fashion for northern Europeans escaping winter. Corso Umberto, the main street, is pedestrian and lined with shops, cafes and little churches, and in high season it is crowded.

That matters to a rider. Parking in the centre is tightly controlled, and large vehicles are kept out of the old town, so use a car park at the edge and walk in. The road up from the coast is a series of hairpins with sea views, and the last kilometres can be busy with coaches and taxis, so avoid mid-afternoon in July and August. Spring and autumn are the best times, with warm light and fewer people. Early evening is the moment when the sun lights Etna from the side.

For food, Sicily is rarely a disappointment. Order granita with a brioche for breakfast, arancini in the afternoon, and pasta with fresh sardines or swordfish in the evening. Cannoli is the sweet to try. Fuel is available in the lower town and on the coastal road, and the stations are easy to find. Taormina is a place to end a ride slowly, with a glass of Etna wine and a long look at the volcano.
t.dune 45@-24.7,15.5:
Dune 45 is a long, curving ridge of red sand in the Namib, forty-five kilometres from the Sesriem gate on the road to Sossusvlei, and the numbering explains its name. It stands about 170 metres high and its sharp crest has become the best-known dune in Namibia. The red colour comes from iron in the sand, which oxidises over time, so the older the dune, the redder it is. In the first light of the morning, it glows orange against a blue-black sky, and in the late afternoon the shadow side turns the colour of charcoal. The dune is not the tallest in the desert, but it is the one most people climb, because it is the easiest to reach.

The paved road that brings you here is a long, quiet, straight one with a few gentle bends, running through a flat, pale desert plain. On both sides you see the dune sea rising in the distance, and you pass solitary camel thorn trees, springbok, oryx and, if you are lucky, an ostrich. Because the park gates open at around sunrise and close at sunset, most visitors arrive together in the morning. If you arrive earlier or later, the road can be almost empty. Wind picks up through the morning and sand can blow across the tarmac in streaks, so watch for patches of drift when the gusts are strong.

The Namib is considered one of the oldest deserts in the world, and its dunes are shaped by winds blowing in from the Atlantic. Fog rolls in off the cold ocean, and the plants and beetles that live here have learned to drink it. The climb up Dune 45 takes a bit of effort in soft sand, and it is best done at sunrise before the heat sets in. Take water, wear sun protection, and leave the helmet and riding boots at the bottom.

Sesriem, at the gate, offers fuel, and Solitaire, on the road to the north, is a well-known stop with a petrol pump and a famous apple pie; even so, it is wise to arrive with a full tank and some spare, because distances are large. Temperatures swing from cold at dawn to very hot by midday. A buff or scarf against the dust is a good idea.
t.sossusvlei@-24.7,15.3:
Sossusvlei means something like the dead-end marsh, and that is exactly what it is: a clay pan where the Tsauchab river, in the rare years when it flows, runs out of strength and disappears into the dunes. For most of the time the pan is white, cracked and dry, surrounded by some of the tallest sand dunes on earth, including the one known as Big Daddy, rising roughly three hundred metres above the floor. Everything about the place is on a giant scale, and the silence is huge. The smell, if you stop and stand still, is of warm dust and nothing else.

The tarmac road leads about sixty kilometres from the Sesriem gate and finishes at a car park, from which the last few kilometres are soft sand that needs a four-wheel drive or a shuttle. A big road bike should stay at the car park, and so should anything that depends on a good grip. Some riders walk the last stretch, which takes an hour or so each way in heat, and there is no shelter. Take water, a hat and sunscreen, and do not underestimate the sun. The Namib offers a lot of beauty but little forgiveness.

Close to the pan lies Deadvlei, a smaller white clay pan where the skeletons of camel thorn trees stand, black against the red dunes and the blue sky. The trees are said to be around nine hundred years old and have been dead for a long time, preserved by the dry air. It is among the most photographed places in Africa, and with good reason. Go early, when the shadows are long and the crowds are small.

Distances are the thing to plan. Sesriem, at the park entrance, has a fuel station and a small shop, but supplies can be limited, so carry what you need and fill up whenever you can. The nearest big towns are very far away. Wind blows sand across the road in the afternoons, so ride with care, and be wary of oryx and springbok that step out onto the tarmac. The park is dark at night and no place to be riding after dusk. Sleep at Sesriem and wake before sunrise.
t.deadvlei@-24.8,15.3:
Deadvlei is a white clay pan in the heart of the Namib desert, ringed by some of the tallest dunes on earth, and it looks like a stage set. The pan holds a scatter of camel thorn trees that died perhaps nine hundred years ago, when the river that fed the area changed course and sand blocked its path. The trees have not rotted in the dry air, and they stand blackened by the sun against the white floor and the orange dunes, which is the photograph everyone wants. Sossusvlei, the larger pan, is a short distance away, and Big Daddy, a dune about 325 metres high, rises beside Deadvlei. There are no towns for a very long way.

The ride to Sossusvlei is along a tarred road from Sesriem, about sixty kilometres long, which runs through the park as the dunes grow larger and redder. The last few kilometres to Deadvlei are a sandy track suited only to four-wheel drive, with a shuttle available from a car park, so riders usually leave their bikes at the paved end and walk or take the shuttle. The walk to the pan from the track takes about fifteen minutes over loose sand. Heat is a serious hazard, as the desert sun is fierce and shade is rare.

Sesriem, at the park entrance, has fuel, a campsite and a lodge, but little else, so you should have your tank full and carry water. The gates open at sunrise and close at sunset, and entry is paid. To see the dunes at their best, arrive at dawn, when the sand glows deep red and the shadows are long, and the temperature is pleasant. By midday, the pan is baking, and there is no reason to stay.

Life is present, if you look. Beetles, geckos and snakes live among the dunes, and oryx and springbok walk the pans. Fog from the Atlantic brings enough moisture for some plants and insects, which drink the condensation. The Namib is thought to be the oldest desert in the world, and the silence is thick. Take nothing and leave nothing, and give yourself time to simply sit.
t.rudnaya pristan@44.4,135.8:
Rudnaya Pristan is a small port on the Sea of Japan, set at the mouth of the Rudnaya River on the rugged coast of northern Primorsky Krai. The name means ore landing, and it tells you what the place is for. For decades the lead and zinc concentrate mined and processed in Dalnegorsk, about twenty-seven kilometres inland, has been trucked down the valley and loaded onto ships here. About two and a half thousand people live in the town, and the working harbour dominates the view, with cranes, storage sheds and the occasional bulk carrier waiting at anchor.

The road from Dalnegorsk follows the river downstream between steep, forested hills, and it is a surprisingly pleasant ride on a quiet day. The surface is mixed, with good asphalt and some rough patches caused by heavy trucks, and the corners are moderate with the odd tight bend near the coast. Ore lorries are the main traffic, so keep right on blind curves and give them room. In summer the valley is warm and humid, with fog rolling in from the sea; in autumn the weather clears, and the hillsides turn gold and red. Winters are cold with snow, and the coast is exposed to harsh north winds.

Services are modest in the port, but enough for a stop: a few shops, a small cafe or two, and a couple of places to buy fuel, though you should not rely on them late in the evening. Dalnegorsk, with more than thirty-eight thousand people, is the real centre, with larger shops, a market and proper garages. Fill the tank there, buy food and water, and treat Rudnaya Pristan as the place where you reach the sea rather than a place to stock up.

Dalnegorsk has a surprising claim to fame. On a winter night in 1986 residents reported a glowing object over a hill outside town, which is still known as Height 611, and the story has become one of the best-known UFO tales in Russia. Whatever you make of it, the hills here have a strange atmosphere, especially at dusk, when mist gathers in the valleys and the sea beyond turns the colour of pewter. Take a few minutes at the shore, listen to the gulls and cranes, and then turn back up the river.
t.plastun@44.8,136.3:
Plastun is a fishing and logging settlement of about six thousand people on the coast of the Sea of Japan, in the northern part of Primorsky Krai, and it is the doorway to the Sikhote-Alin Nature Reserve. The reserve, founded in the 1930s, was created to protect the sable and later became one of the key refuges of the Amur tiger. Much of it lies in the mountains behind the settlement, and the coastline below it is a long strip of rocky headlands, pebble beaches and river mouths, backed by forest that comes down almost to the water.

The ride up the coast from Dalnegorsk is long, quiet and rewarding. The road is a mix of reasonable asphalt and rough patches, with gradients that come in short, steep bursts as it crosses spurs from the mountains, and corners that tighten on the descents to river valleys. Traffic is light, apart from the occasional logging truck, and there are few places to stop for services, so plan fuel carefully. Summer is warm and wet, with fog and drizzle; autumn is the best season, with dry days and spectacular colour. Winter brings snow, ice and strong winds, and the road may be hard going.

In Plastun itself, you will find shops, a few cafes, a petrol station and basic accommodation, enough to rest and refuel. Kamenka, the last sizeable village to the south, is about forty kilometres back and smaller than you might expect, so fill the tank here before heading on to Terney. Local fish, especially salmon in season and smoked fish at the market, is the thing to try, and the tea is strong and hot.

The reserve is not a place you can ride into, but its edge gives a feel for what is protected. Tigers, bears, lynx and sika deer all live in the forests, and the rivers carry salmon in the autumn run, drawing eagles and, now and then, brown bears. Even from the road you may notice the quality of the forest, with Korean pine and oak, vines winding through the trees, and ferns in the shade. Watch for animals at dusk and dawn, keep your speed moderate, and leave the engine off for a minute when you stop, because the quiet is worth hearing.
t.khandyga@62.7,135.6:
Khandyga is a town of nearly seven thousand people on the Aldan River in the Sakha Republic, and it is one of the key points on the Kolyma Highway between Yakutsk and the Pacific coast. The country around it is eastern Siberia at its most characteristic: wide river terraces, larch and pine forest, and the long blue line of the Verkhoyansk Range along the horizon. Winters here are among the coldest in the northern hemisphere, with the rivers frozen for more than half the year, and the highway often runs on ice in places.

In Soviet times, Khandyga was also a camp settlement, part of the system that built the roads and mines of the north, and the Kolyma Highway that passes through it carries that heavy memory. If you ride here with some knowledge of the history, the long straight road and the empty forest take on a different tone. The wind sighs in the larches, the river runs wide and slow, and the sense of the past hangs in the air.

The road to Khandyga from Yakutsk is a long ride in itself, requiring a crossing of the Lena and then a push across the plateau. The route involves ferries in summer and ice crossings in winter, and you should check the schedules and conditions before you go, as they change from year to year. The surface is a mix of asphalt and gravel, with some good sections and some very rough ones, and rain can make the clay roads treacherous. Bring spares, extra fuel and food, and a flexible schedule. The best months are June to September.

With its size, Khandyga has fuel, shops, cafes and basic accommodation, and it is the place to stock up before pushing further east. The market sells local fish, including the freshwater whitefish found in the rivers, and meat dishes are the staple. Take a walk along the riverbank at dusk, when the mosquitoes are busy and the light is long and soft. Keep your gear dry, your tank full and your plans loose, and you will find that this far corner of Yakutia rewards patient riders with a sense of real distance.
t.necropolis of pantalica@37.1,15.0:
Thousands of small square doorways riddle the limestone cliffs above the Anapo and Calcinara valleys, like the windows of a vast abandoned apartment block. These are rock-cut tombs, some five thousand of them, carved by the people who lived at Pantalica between roughly the thirteenth and seventh centuries before Christ. Together with Syracuse, the necropolis is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and it is one of the most evocative places in Sicily, in a gorge of the Hyblaean Mountains west of Syracuse, between the towns of Sortino and Ferla.

The settlement here was large and powerful before the Greeks arrived to found Syracuse, and the remains of a building often called the Anaktoron, the prince's palace, crown the plateau. Later, in the Byzantine period, some tombs were enlarged into small dwellings and chapels, a few with traces of frescoes. The gorge below is now a nature reserve, with a clear river, pools, plane trees and oleanders, and trails along the old railway line that once ran through the valley. In spring the slopes are bright with wildflowers and the air hums with bees.

The roads in are part of the pleasure. From Sortino, a narrow road winds down to the northern edge of the necropolis, while from Ferla another approaches from the west and ends at viewpoints over the gorge; the two do not connect by road, so choose your side or plan a long loop. Both are twisty, with patchy surfaces, sharp bends and occasional livestock. The wider Hyblaean plateau offers excellent riding, linking baroque towns such as Palazzolo Acreide, Noto and Modica on quiet back roads with stone walls and carob trees.

Sortino, a town of around eight and a half thousand, has fuel and basic services, and it is known for its honey, harvested from the thyme and orange blossom of the hills. Carry plenty of water, because summer heat is intense and the trails offer little shade. Then reward yourself with a granita or a cannolo in town, where pastry is taken almost as seriously as history.
t.mount etna@37.8,15.0:
Etna is not so much a mountain as a living presence that dominates eastern Sicily. Europe's highest active volcano rises over 3,300 metres above Catania, its height changing as eruptions add and remove material, and it smokes, rumbles and occasionally spits fire with a regularity that the locals regard with a mix of reverence and resignation.

The eastern slopes are fertile and green, with vineyards, orchards and chestnut woods thriving on the volcanic soils. In Sant'Alfio grows the Castagno dei Cento Cavalli, an ancient chestnut tree said to be the oldest in Europe, whose name comes from a legend about a queen sheltering beneath it with a hundred knights during a storm. Zafferana is known for honey and its annual festival of Etna produce, and it has had close calls with lava; in 1992 a flow was diverted to save the town. Etna's wines, especially the Nerello Mascalese reds, have become prized in recent years.

The roads up the mountain are some of the best in Sicily, with long sequences of bends winding through forests and across stark black lava fields. From Zafferana and Milo, roads climb to the south side and the Rifugio Sapienza at around 1,900 metres, where cable cars and jeeps head higher. On the north side, the Mareneve road links Linguaglossa, Milo and Piano Provenzana. Surfaces vary, and volcanic ash can make the roads slippery after eruptions. In winter snow covers the upper slopes, and in summer the cooler air is a relief from the coastal heat. Mornings are clearest before cloud builds around the summit.

Zafferana Etnea has fuel, cafés and restaurants, and is a good base on this side of the mountain. Higher up, the Rifugio Sapienza has restaurants and souvenir stands. Check the volcano's status before you go, as eruptions can close roads and restrict access to the summit areas. Bring warm clothing, since even in summer temperatures drop sharply with altitude, and enjoy granita and brioche back down in the villages.
t.catania@37.5,15.1:
Catania has been knocked down and rebuilt so many times that it has made a style out of resilience. Lava from Etna overran parts of the city in 1669, and then in 1693 a devastating earthquake flattened it almost entirely. The rebuilding produced one of the most striking Baroque cities in Italy, built with dark grey lava stone set off against pale limestone, with wide straight streets designed to offer escape routes in future disasters. The centre is part of the Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto World Heritage Site, and Etna looms over everything, often smoking at the end of the Via Etnea.

In the Piazza del Duomo stands the city's symbol, a lava-stone elephant carrying an Egyptian obelisk, known affectionately as u Liotru. The cathedral holds the relics of Saint Agatha, the patron saint, whose festival in early February brings huge crowds onto the streets for days. The composer Vincenzo Bellini was born here, and his name graces the opera house, a park and a pastry or two. The fish market, la Pescheria, behind the cathedral, is a riot of noise, colour and swordfish heads every morning except Sunday.

Riding in Catania itself is an exercise in assertiveness: traffic is chaotic, scooters weave in every gap, the cobbles are slippery when wet and parking is creative. But the city is a gateway to some of the best riding in Sicily. The roads up Etna, from Nicolosi to the Rifugio Sapienza or around the north side through Linguaglossa, are superb, and south towards Siracusa and the Baroque towns of Noto, Modica and Ragusa, the Iblei hills offer twisting roads and wonderful views.

Petrol, tyres and mechanics are easy to find in a city this size, and the food alone justifies an overnight stop. Locals will argue that the fried rice ball here is the masculine arancino rather than the Palermo arancina; pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and salted ricotta, is named after Bellini's opera; and summer breakfast means almond or pistachio granita with a soft brioche to dip. Keep valuables off the bike, use a guarded garage overnight, and be ready for the volcano to dust everything, including your visor, with fine black grit after an eruption.
t.epipolae@37.1,15.2:
Above Syracuse the land rises in a long limestone terrace, a triangle of high ground pointing inland, and the ancient Greeks called it Epipolae, the place above the city. Whoever held it held Syracuse. During the great Athenian expedition against the city, between 415 and 413 BC, the fight for this plateau decided the war: the Athenians tried to wall Syracuse in from here, the Syracusans and their Spartan allies built counter-walls, and in the end the Athenian army was destroyed, with thousands of prisoners left to die in the stone quarries below. A few years later the tyrant Dionysius I enclosed the entire plateau with walls many kilometres long, and at its western tip he built the Castello Eurialo, one of the most complete Greek fortresses anywhere.

The Euryalus fort is the place to stop. It has moats cut into the bedrock, towers and a maze of underground passages that let defenders move unseen, and from the top you can look east over the modern sprawl of Syracuse to the sea and the island of Ortigia, the old heart of the city. On a clear day Etna appears to the north. The surrounding land is a patchwork of dry-stone walls, olive and carob trees and wild fennel, and in spring the plateau is full of flowers.

Riding out of Syracuse, this is the first climb, and it leads to excellent things. The SS124 heads west into the Hyblaean Mountains, a limestone upland cut by deep gorges, towards Palazzolo Acreide with its baroque churches and Greek theatre, and beyond to the rock-cut tombs of Pantalica. The roads are often narrow and twisty, with rough patches, walls right at the edge of the lane and very little traffic. South, the baroque towns of the Val di Noto, Noto, Modica and Scicli, rebuilt after the earthquake of 1693, make a wonderful loop, and Scicli will be familiar to anyone who has watched the Montalbano television series.

Belvedere, the suburb that sits right on the plateau, has fuel, bars and shops, and Syracuse below has everything. Spend the evening in Ortigia, with its Greek temple of Apollo, the spring of Arethusa full of papyrus, and seafood by the water. In the morning, an almond granita with a brioche is the proper Sicilian breakfast before the heat of the day.
t.royal domain of drottningholm@59.3,17.9:
The Swedish royal family does not live in Stockholm's city palace; since 1981 its home has been Drottningholm, a baroque palace on the island of Lovön in Lake Mälaren, a short ride west of the capital. The name means the queen's islet, and the present palace was begun in the 1660s for the widowed Queen Hedvig Eleonora, designed by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder and finished by his son. With its formal gardens, fountains and an English landscape park, it is often compared to Versailles, though it is far more intimate. Parts of the palace are open to visitors, and the whole royal domain is a World Heritage site.

The real treasure is the palace theatre, built in 1766, which still has its original stage machinery: wooden wave machines, cloud cars, trapdoors and painted backdrops that can be changed in seconds, all operated by hand. Operas from the eighteenth century are still performed there in summer, and it is one of the very few theatres of its time anywhere to survive in working order. In the park, the Chinese Pavilion, a rococo fantasy of the East built as a birthday surprise for Queen Lovisa Ulrika, is another delight.

The ride out from Stockholm along Drottningholmsvägen crosses bridges and islands, with water glittering on both sides, and once on Lovön and the larger island of Ekerö the roads become quiet country lanes through farmland, forest and small villages, with the lake always close by. Further on, a free road ferry crosses to Adelsö, where the royal estate of Hovgården, with its burial mounds and rune stone, faces Björkö and the Viking town of Birka, which can only be reached by boat. Swedish roads are excellent, but speed cameras are everywhere and fines are high, so keep an eye on the limits. Elk and deer can cross at dawn and dusk.

Bromma and Ekerö both have fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and Stockholm is close. There is a café at the palace, and summer kiosks along the lake sell coffee and the cinnamon buns that are practically a national institution, ideal for a fika, the Swedish coffee break. The best time to visit is from late spring to early autumn, when the gardens are in full bloom and the long northern evenings stay light until late.
t.ortygia@37.1,15.3:
Ortygia is the island where Syracuse began. Greek colonists from Corinth landed here in 734 BC, drawn by a harbour and a freshwater spring, and the town they founded grew into the most powerful city in the Greek world, rivalling Athens. The island is small enough to walk across in fifteen minutes and holds an astonishing density of history. The cathedral is built into the columns of a Greek temple of Athena, so the Doric pillars are still visible in its walls. A few steps away, the freshwater spring of Arethusa still bubbles up beside the sea, with papyrus plants growing in the pool.

Archimedes lived here, and the Roman general Marcellus took the city after a long siege in 212 BC, with his orders reportedly to spare the great mathematician, who was killed anyway. Later centuries brought Byzantines, Arabs, Normans and Spanish, and the baroque rebuilding after the earthquake of 1693 gave the island its honey-coloured piazzas.

For a rider, Ortygia is lovely but awkward. The island is mostly a restricted traffic zone, and its lanes are narrow and full of people, so leave the bike in a car park on the mainland near the bridge and walk across. Syracuse itself is a busy city of nearly a hundred thousand with pumps all around, and you will find fuel before you reach the island. The market near the Temple of Apollo in the morning is full of swordfish, tomatoes, capers and cheese, and the stalls will sell you a sandwich that does the job of lunch.

The rest of south-east Sicily is excellent for riding. The roads toward Noto and Scicli run through limestone country, with carob trees, dry stone walls and the bright baroque towns of the Val di Noto, and the surface varies from smooth to rough. Spring is the best season, with wildflowers and warm days, while August is too hot for comfort. Wind can blow strongly along the coast.

Evening is the best moment for Ortygia, when the stone glows, the sea turns pink and the lanes fill with the smell of grilled fish.
t.syracuse and the rocky necropolis of pan:
Syracuse is far more than the island of Ortygia. The mainland district of Neapolis holds the Greek theatre, carved into the hillside and still used for classical drama in early summer, and the Latomie, the huge quarries from which the Greeks cut their stone, now filled with citrus trees and overhung with cliffs. The most famous cavity is the Ear of Dionysius, a tall curved cave with remarkable acoustics, which Caravaggio is said to have named when he visited in 1608. The same painter's Burial of Saint Lucy hangs in Syracuse too, dark and physical, with two gravediggers in the foreground dwarfing the saint.

The second half of the heritage listing sits well inland. Pantalica is a limestone plateau cut by the deep gorges of the Anapo and Calcinara rivers, and its cliffs are riddled with thousands of rock-cut tombs, small square chambers dug into the face from about the thirteenth century BC onward. Nobody knows exactly who the people were, but they lived on the high plateau as a fortified settlement, long before the Greeks arrived on the coast. The scale of the cemetery, row on row of dark openings, is unsettling.

Getting there is half the pleasure. The road from Syracuse leads through Floridia and Sortino, and then enters hills of carob and olive and oak, with views of the gorge. The last miles are narrow, steep and sometimes rough, and the surface can be broken after rain. A part of the old railway that served the valley now forms a footpath.

Syracuse has all the fuel and food a rider needs, and a city of nearly a hundred thousand people has pumps on every approach. Before leaving, try a granita made with almond or mulberry and a brioche for breakfast in the Sicilian manner, which will keep you going.

Further south, the papyrus plants along the Ciane river are another curious thing. They are often described as the only wild stand of papyrus in Europe.
t.birka@59.3,17.5:
A thousand years ago, you could have bought a silk scarf, a bag of silver coins and a slave on a small island in Lake Malaren, and a visitor from Byzantium would have felt at home. Birka, on the island of Bjorko, west of Stockholm, was the first real town in Sweden, founded around 750 and abandoned about two centuries later, and it was a market where Vikings met traders from the Frankish lands, the Baltic and as far away as the Arab world. Archaeologists have found coins from the Caliphate, beads from the east and glass from the Rhineland. Several thousand graves lie on the hillsides around the site, most of them simple mounds in the grass, and more of them have been opened than you might think.

The best-known one is the grave of a warrior buried with swords, arrowheads, a shield and two horses, which was long assumed to belong to a man. In 2017, DNA analysis showed that the skeleton was a woman, and the finding stirred a lively debate among scholars about the roles of women in Viking society that continues. Birka's most famous Christian visitor was the monk Ansgar, who came to preach in about 829, a mission that had little lasting success. The town's decline may have been linked to the silting of the harbour, as the land rose after the Ice Age, and Sigtuna took over as the main centre. Birka and the nearby royal estate of Hovgarden were listed as World Heritage in 1993.

You cannot ride to the island, which is only reached by boat, and in the summer season there are excursions from Stockholm that take a couple of hours each way. That makes the stop part of a day trip rather than a road, and the mainland side is a pleasure in its own right. From Stockholm, the roads west run through Ekero and the islands of Lake Malaren, with fields, oak woods and red wooden farmhouses, low traffic outside rush hours and a speed limit enforced by cameras. Swedish drivers are courteous, and the roads are well maintained.

Ekero, sixteen kilometres from the site by the map, has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and Stockholm has all you could want. The island itself has a small museum, a cafe and a few waymarked paths, and a visit takes a few hours. Midsummer, in late June, brings nights that are barely dark, and early autumn brings clear air and colour. Take a warm layer, since the breeze off the lake can be cool even in July, and bring your own water.
t.hovga rden@59.4,17.5:
The kings of the Svear lived here, on the island of Adelso in Lake Malaren, and their hall stood on a ridge from which they could watch the water traffic to Birka. Hovgarden means the court farm, and the name hints at what it was: a royal manor, the seat of power for the region in the Viking Age, set directly across a narrow channel from the island that held the trading town. The site is known today for the Kungshogarna, the royal mounds, a row of large grave mounds along the ridge, from the Iron Age and Viking Age, which are among the most visible reminders of Sweden's early kings, and for a runestone and a medieval church, built in the twelfth century, that stands on the highest point.

Together with Birka, the farm was listed as a World Heritage site in 1993, as a picture of a trade and power system that stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea. The landscape is gentle, with fields, grazing cattle, oak trees and the lake on all sides, and the church tower, painted white, serves as a landmark. In summer, the wild flowers on the mounds are a delight, and in the evening the light from the lake turns the grass gold.

Adelso is reached by a short road ferry, which means a motorbike can roll straight on and off, and the crossing itself is part of the fun. On the island, the roads are narrow and lightly used, lined with farms and woods, and a quiet circuit takes you past the church and the mounds. The ride this stop belongs to carries on to Drottningholm, the royal palace on the neighbouring island of Lovon, begun in the seventeenth century in the style of Versailles and now a residence of the royal family, with a baroque theatre from the eighteenth century that still has its original stage machinery, and a Chinese pavilion in the park. The palace is also a World Heritage site.

Ekero, eighteen kilometres away by the map, has fuel and shops, and the area is within easy reach of Stockholm. Cafes in the area serve cinnamon buns and strong coffee, a Swedish ritual called fika, and a stop in the afternoon fits the mood of the place. Check the ferry timetable, which changes by season, and avoid the busiest summer weekends if you can, when cyclists and day trippers crowd the island. Spring and early autumn are the best times, and midsummer evenings can be lovely.
t.kuiseb pass@-23.3,15.8:
The Kuiseb is a river that mostly isn't. For most of the year its bed is a broad strip of dry sand, lined with ana trees and camelthorn, running west from the Namibian highlands toward Walvis Bay, and only after heavy rain in the interior does water come down it, sometimes in a brown flood that reaches the sea. Along its course, the river has cut a deep canyon through the edge of the plateau, and the road, the C26, drops through it at Kuiseb Pass, at about 905 metres, in a series of bends with views over rocky ridges and dry valleys.

The canyon has a story attached. During the Second World War, two German geologists, Henno Martin and Hermann Korn, evaded internment by retreating into the desert, and for more than two years lived in a rock shelter near the Kuiseb, hunting game and drinking from springs. Martin later wrote a book about it, The Sheltering Desert, which is a classic of survival and of the desert's strange beauty. Not far away, the Gobabeb research station has studied the Namib since the 1960s, and its work on fog, beetles and dune life is known around the world.

The landscape is stark and lovely. To the north lie gravel plains and low hills, to the south the great sand sea of the Namib, with dunes that run on for hundreds of kilometres. The colours change through the day, from pale gold at dawn to deep orange at sunset. Wildlife is thin but present, with oryx, springbok and the occasional zebra on the plains, and the dry riverbed is a corridor for animals and birds.

The road surface is gravel, hard-packed in places and loose in others, with corrugations and sandy patches, and speed should be kept moderate. In the dry bed of the river, there may be soft sand at crossings. Fuel is the key problem. Walvis Bay, on the coast, has full services, and Solitaire, a tiny settlement to the east, has a petrol station, a bakery known for its apple pie and a few wrecked cars as decoration, but nothing in between, so fill up and carry extra. Carry plenty of water, since the climate is dry and the sun intense. Nights are cold, and mornings can be misty near the coast.
t.gamsberg pass@-23.3,16.2:
Gamsberg is an odd mountain, a huge flat-topped block of rock that rises abruptly from the plains of the Khomas Hochland, almost 2,350 metres high, and it can be seen from kilometres away. It is an inselberg, a survivor of an older landscape that has been worn down around it, and its pale sides, glowing red in the evening, dominate the horizon. The pass that takes its name, at 1,665 metres, is on the road from the coast to Windhoek, and it marks the point where the land drops from the highland plateau toward the Namib desert.

The Khomas Hochland is a high, rolling country of grass and thornbush, cut by gullies, where the farms are huge and the farmhouses far apart. The names on the signs are German, a reminder of the colonial settlers who took up land here in the early twentieth century, and cattle and game farms are the main activity. The air is dry, clear and bright, and the sky is a deep blue. On the night of a new moon, the stars are so thick that the Milky Way casts a faint shadow. Not far from the Gamsberg, a group of large telescopes, built to detect gamma rays from space, takes advantage of that dark sky.

The pass itself has switchbacks and steep sections, with views opening across the valley, and a sheer drop on one side. The road, the C26, is gravel, and its condition varies with the season and recent grading. After rain, it can be slippery and cut by washouts, while in dry weather it is corrugated and dusty. Ride at a moderate speed, keep a good distance from other vehicles because of the dust and watch for livestock on the road. Baboons often sit on the rocks by the roadside, and kudu and mountain zebra graze on the slopes.

Plan your tank carefully, and carry spare fuel in a jerrycan. Water is a necessity, and a first aid kit, tools and a means of calling for help are wise. Weather is usually dry, but summer storms can bring flash floods in the gullies. The best months are from May to September, when the days are warm and the nights cold, and the light is superb.
t.cozzo ferriero@39.9,16.1:
Pollino is the biggest national park in Italy, a high limestone massif on the border between Calabria and Basilicata, where the southern Apennines make their last great stand before the toe of the peninsula. The summits reach over two thousand metres, with Serra Dolcedorme at 2,267, and on the exposed ridges grow the pino loricato, the Bosnian pine, a tree of extraordinary age, twisted by wind into sculptural shapes, with some individuals said to be a thousand years old. Griffon vultures and eagles patrol the cliffs, and the wolf has returned to the forests.

Cozzo Ferriero lies in this high country, near Rotonda and Viggianello, on the Basilicata side, and the name, which means something like iron hill, is typical of the region. The villages are small, with stone houses and steep lanes, and the local culture mixes Italian and ancient traditions, with some communities nearby speaking Arbëreshë, a form of Albanian brought by refugees in the fifteenth century.

Roads in the Pollino are rewarding, with curves, forests and long views over the valleys, and few other riders. The surface is mixed, with good main roads and rough minor ones, and rock fall and landslides happen after storms. Spring brings wildflowers and meltwater, summer is warm but breezy at height, and autumn colours the beech woods. Snow can close the high roads from late autumn to spring, and the weather can change fast, with fog on the ridges.

Rotonda has about seventeen hundred people and Viggianello fewer than five hundred, so services are limited. Fill the tank at Lauria or Castrovillari, the bigger towns, before you climb, and carry some food. Local specialities include sausages flavoured with the sweet pepper of the region, cheeses, and the peperoni cruschi, crisp dried peppers. The ride goes on toward the Cilento and the Vallo di Diano, another great park, so the day is long and the scenery rich.
t.uppsala@59.9,17.6:
Uppsala is a university town on the Fyris River, about seventy kilometres north of Stockholm, and its centre of gravity is the cathedral. It is the largest church in Scandinavia, with towers that rise to over a hundred metres, built of brick in a French Gothic style from the late thirteenth century onward. Swedish kings were crowned and buried in it, including Gustav Vasa, the founder of the modern kingdom, and so was the scientist and philosopher Emanuel Swedenborg. Carl Linnaeus, the man who gave plants and animals their two-part Latin names, is also buried here, and his garden, a short walk away, is kept as he planted it.

The university, founded in 1477, is the oldest in the Nordic countries, and it gives the town its character of cyclists, students, bookshops and red-brick buildings. On the last night of April, Walpurgis Eve, students gather along the river in white caps to sing and drink, and the town is lively. The Carolina Rediviva library holds the Codex Argenteus, the Silver Bible, a sixth-century Gothic manuscript written in silver and gold ink on purple parchment, which is one of the most precious books in Europe.

Just north of town lies Gamla Uppsala, Old Uppsala, where three great burial mounds stand on the plain. They date from the fifth and sixth centuries and are traditionally linked to early Swedish kings. In the Viking Age, a famous temple stood nearby, described by the medieval writer Adam of Bremen, who told of a sacrifice held every nine years. The mounds are quiet and grassy, and a small church and museum stand beside them. It is a place that rewards a slow walk.

The ride south to Drottningholm, the royal palace on an island in Lake Malaren, follows quiet roads through farmland and along bays, with views of water. The route is flat, with gentle bends and limited traffic. Wind from the lake can be cool. In Uppsala, parking for motorbikes is easy near the centre, and fuel stations are on the ring road. Traffic cameras are common in Sweden, and limits are strict.

Eat a kanelbulle, a cinnamon bun, in one of the old cafes by the river. Summer evenings are long, and the best months are May to September.
t.stockholm@59.3,18.1:
Stockholm is built on fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic, and water is always in view. The old town, Gamla Stan, sits on a small island at the centre, a knot of cobbled lanes, ochre and red façades and narrow courtyards that dates back to the thirteenth century, with the huge royal palace and the cathedral at its heart. In 1520 the Danish king had dozens of Swedish nobles beheaded in the main square, the Stockholm Bloodbath, and the event helped to spark the rebellion that placed Gustav Vasa on the throne. These days the square is a pretty place for coffee, and the shop windows are full of Dala horses and candles.

The best museum for a rider with an eye for engineering is the Vasa, which houses a warship that sank on its maiden voyage in 1628, after sailing barely a kilometre, because it was top-heavy. It lay on the harbour bottom for more than three centuries and was raised in 1961 almost complete, and the ship is astonishing, a towering carved and painted hull that still smells of wood and tar. Out beyond the city the archipelago stretches for thousands of islands, with red wooden cabins, ferries and sailing boats, and the white summer evenings when the sun barely sets are a time of long dinners on the water.

Riding in Stockholm is straightforward, though bridges and tunnels make navigation interesting, and the ring roads and the E4 motorway can be busy at rush hour. Speed limits are strictly enforced by cameras, and Swedes drive with calm discipline. The best riding lies outside the city, on the lanes north through the Uppland plain with its runestones, farms and red barns, or along the coast road past old estates and lakes. In summer the roads are open and dry, and the evenings are long, but in winter ice and snow make riding unwise.

Fuel is plentiful in and around the city, with stations on every approach, though some are unmanned and require a card, so carry one that works in Sweden. Fika, the coffee and cinnamon bun break, is a national habit and a good way to rest between rides. The ferries to the islands are part of the public transport and are worth a trip on a sunny day.
t.alpine@30.4,-103.7:
Alpine lies in the high desert of West Texas, at roughly 4,500 feet, in a basin between the Davis Mountains to the north and the long, empty country that runs south toward Big Bend. It is a railroad and ranching town of just under six thousand that has quietly become the logical base for anyone heading into the park, and also a college town, because Sul Ross State University sits on a hill above the main street. The result is better coffee than you would expect at the end of a long highway.

The place feels like the hinge of the region. Marfa, with its art-world reputation and its mysterious lights, is about thirty-five kilometres west, and Fort Davis, the old frontier army post under the mountains, is about the same distance north. The scenic loop through the Davis Mountains is a very good ride, climbing and twisting through volcanic rock with real elevation change in a country that otherwise looks flat. South from Alpine, Texas 118 runs about a hundred miles through ranch country, past Study Butte and Terlingua, the old quicksilver mining town turned ghost town turned chili-cookoff, before reaching the park entrance.

Riding here is about distance and light. The roads are long, straight, wide and quiet, with the occasional gentle swell and a crosswind that can lean on you hard. Surfaces are generally good, but cattle guards, livestock and wildlife on the road are common, and javelinas and deer are active at dusk. Summer afternoons are fierce, with temperatures that make a full jacket an act of faith, so start early and carry more water than you think you need. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter mornings can be properly cold at this elevation, though usually clear and bright.

This is the place to fill the tank and the water bottles, because services thin out south of here. There is fuel in town and several places for food, from tacos to burgers, and the stretch to the park has only a few stops, so do not gamble on the needle. Once you ride out of Alpine heading south, the sky gets enormous and the mountains give way to the Chihuahuan Desert. It is a good problem to have.
t.sesriem@-24.5,15.8:
Sesriem is the gate to the great dunes of the Namib, a tiny settlement of a campsite, a lodge and a filling station, set on a gravel plain beneath a sky that is nearly always blue. The name means six thongs: early settlers had to tie six lengths of ox-hide together to draw water from a narrow canyon nearby, and the canyon, a slot about thirty metres deep carved by the Tsauchab River, is the first sight you meet. The river itself rarely flows, but when it does, in good rain years, it sends water out toward Sossusvlei and fills the pans with a thin blue sheet.

The dunes are the main reason anyone comes. Stretching southward from the Tsauchab, a sea of red sand reaches up to some three hundred metres, among the tallest in the world, and they change colour through the day, from pink at dawn to deep orange at midday and purple at dusk. A paved road runs sixty kilometres from the Sesriem gate to Sossusvlei, passing Dune 45, a favourite for sunrise photographs, and then a track continues to the pans. Deadvlei, a white clay pan with the blackened skeletons of camel thorn trees, some of them six hundred years old, is a favourite.

The ride in is a gravel road, with long stretches of corrugations, loose gravel and soft sand, and the main hazards are the surface, the distance and the heat. The temperature swings from near freezing before dawn to thirty-five or more at midday, so dress in layers. The park gates open at sunrise and close at sunset, and the best light is in the first hour. Wind can pick up in the afternoon and blows sand across the road.

Sesriem has a station, though supplies can be limited, so fill at Solitaire, a famous roadside stop on the C14 with a bakery known for its apple pie, or in Maltahohe. Carry water, spare fuel, a puncture kit and a tyre pump, and book your camp early, since the sites near the gate fill up. Stay for sunset and sunrise, when the dunes are at their best, and watch the stars come out over the dark desert.
t.dalnegorsk@44.6,135.6:
Dalnegorsk is a mining town of around thirty-eight thousand people in a narrow valley of the Rudnaya River, on the eastern slopes of the Sikhote-Alin, a short distance from the Sea of Japan. It was founded as a lead and zinc centre, and boron production followed, which is why the surrounding hills are scarred with old workings and the local mineral shops sell astonishingly good crystals, including datolite and calcite, from the nearby deposits. Krasnorechenskiy lies a few kilometres away.

Riding in, you come down from the mountain pass on a road that twists through dense forest, with steep slopes and sharp turns, before the valley opens into the town. The surface is variable, with good tarmac mixed with patched sections, and trucks haul ore along some stretches, so expect dust and slow vehicles. It is a lovely ride in autumn, when oak, maple and birch burn red and gold against the dark conifers. Fuel is available in town, and you will want it, since the road to the coast and onward toward Terney has few services.

Dalnegorsk has a fascinating industrial past. Its earlier name was Tetyukhe, after the river, and it was renamed in 1972. Lead-zinc smelting dominated for decades, and the town has a faintly ghostly feel, with large Soviet-era buildings and a landscape shaped by mining. It also has a minor fame in a different field: in January 1986 a strange glowing object was reported near a hill outside town, which became one of Russia's best-known UFO stories, and locals will tell it with a shrug and a smile.

The nature around the valley is extraordinary. The Sikhote-Alin forests shelter Amur tigers, bears, deer and wild boar, and the rivers run cold and clear. The coastline a short ride east has rocky headlands, bays and small fishing villages, with Rudnaya Pristan the main port. The air in the valley smells of pine and, sometimes, of the smelter, but out on the coast it is all salt and cold sea.

For practical purposes, fill the tank, buy food and water, and check the weather. Fog off the sea can be thick, and the roads can be wet and slick. The reward is an authentic, little-visited corner of the Russian Far East.
t.solitaire@-23.9,16.0:
Solitaire is not so much a town as a fuel pump, a cafe and a graveyard of rusting cars in the middle of the Namibian desert, and it is one of the most reliable landmarks on the gravel road between Walvis Bay and Sesriem. The name suits it: there is nothing else for a long way in any direction, only stony plains, camelthorn trees and the far wall of the escarpment. The settlement sits on the edge of the Namib-Naukluft Park, on the C14, where the plateau of central Namibia drops toward the Atlantic.

For a rider, it is a lifeline. There is fuel here, cold drinks, a shop and a bakery that has become a minor legend for its apple pie, and every overlander who passes through seems to stop. Fuel is the key: the nearest alternative is a long way off, and the road conditions make the distances feel longer. The gravel roads around are wide, graded and fast on a good day, but loose stones, sand patches and corrugations can turn a relaxed ride into a wrestling match, and punctures are common. The passes nearby, Spreetshoogte to the north and Kuiseb to the west, drop steeply off the escarpment with tight bends and big views. Early morning is cool and the light is lovely, while the middle of the day is brutally hot.

The landscape is extraordinary. Beyond the settlement, the Namib, one of the oldest deserts in the world, stretches toward the sea, with red dunes, dry riverbeds and mountains of rock that glow at sunset. The desert is home to oryx, springbok, ostrich and small creatures that live on the morning fog, and the sky at night is crammed with stars. The air smells of dust and warm stone, and the silence is almost physical.

The cars rusting beside the pumps are part of the charm, arranged as a kind of art installation, with old Studebakers and trucks fading into the sand. Visitors often photograph them, and the staff are used to riders arriving with dust-caked helmets and a big thirst.

Carry water, spare fuel if you can, and a puncture repair kit. Tell someone your route, since mobile coverage is patchy, and avoid riding at dusk, when wildlife appears on the road.
t.spreetshoogte pass@-23.7,16.2:
Spreetshoogte is the pass that makes you grip the bars a little tighter, and then grin inside your helmet. It drops the Khomas Hochland highlands down to the edge of the Namib desert in one dramatic fall, and it is among the steepest in Namibia, with gradients that reach something like one in seven in places.
