The gravel road is cut into the face of the escarpment, and from the top the view is immense: a plain of red sand and pale grass, flat and empty to the horizon, with the dark lines of the Naukluft mountains running along the south.

The surface is gravel, firm in good conditions but loose on the corners and sometimes badly corrugated at the bottom, so ride it slowly and in a low gear, and let the engine do the braking. Sharp bends and steep drop-offs at the edge leave no margin for error, and a loaded bike is a handful. Loose stones can collect on the inside of the turns, and after rain, streams may cut across the track. Ride in daylight, preferably in the morning when the light is clear and the temperature is bearable, and be aware that the climb is just as challenging in the other direction.

The scenery changes with every few hundred metres of descent. Up high the land is grassy and scattered with acacia, while lower down the vegetation thins and the colours turn to ochre and rust. Dust devils spin in the plain, oryx stand under trees, and on clear evenings the light turns the whole escarpment gold. The temperature difference between top and bottom can be ten degrees, and the wind often picks up in the afternoon.

There is nothing on the pass itself, but Solitaire, a tiny stop on the plain, has fuel, a shop and a bakery famous for its apple pie, and it is the obvious place to refuel and refresh. The dunes of Sossusvlei lie within a day's ride to the south-west, which makes this a natural start or finish to a trip. Carry water, a spare tube and some food, tell someone your plan, and be aware that mobile reception is poor.
t.gamsberg pass@-23.3,16.3:
Seen from the road, the Gamsberg is the sort of mountain a child would draw: a huge flat-topped block of rock standing alone on the plateau, more than 2,300 metres high and nearly three kilometres across at the top. It is one of the landmarks of the Khomas Hochland, the highland region that lies between Windhoek and the Namib desert, and the pass that bears its name carries the road from the plateau down toward the coastal plain, passing the great bulk of the mountain on the way.

The route is part of the gravel highway that connects Windhoek with Walvis Bay, a journey that crosses a sequence of passes as the land steps down from the central highlands to the sea. The Gamsberg Pass is one of the more scenic, with long switchbacks and views down to broad valleys and ridges of dark rock, with isolated farms and empty land stretching out. The road is usually well graded but can be rough and corrugated, and rain can cause washouts, so ride carefully, keep your speed under control, and watch for animals on the road, particularly at dawn and dusk.

The landscape is dry and open, with a sparse cover of thornbush and grass that turns golden after rain. Rock hyrax, baboons and klipspringer live among the boulders, and you may see oryx and kudu near the road, while raptors circle in the thermals above the cliffs. The sky is huge, and the stars at night are spectacular, since the whole region is thinly populated and the air is dry and clear. Daytime temperatures can be high, so start early, and nights are cold in winter.

The nearest services are far away. Fill the tank in Windhoek before setting off, or at Solitaire or Walvis Bay at the other end, and carry water, food and basic spares, since help can be hours away. A handful of guest farms near the pass offer simple meals and rooms, often with stargazing, and it is wise to book in advance and confirm directions. Mobile coverage is patchy, so agree a route with someone and stay on the main road.
t.kuiseb pass@-23.3,15.7:
The Kuiseb River is the line that holds back the dunes. Flowing only after rare rains, it winds across the gravel plains of western Namibia toward Walvis Bay, and for most of its length it forms a natural barrier, with the great sand sea of the Namib to the south and the stony desert to the north. Where the road crosses it, in the Kuiseb canyon, the land drops into a gorge of dark rock, with dry riverbed, acacia and ana trees far below the plain, and the pass is a short, steep ride down and up the other side.

The canyon has a remarkable story. During the Second World War, two German geologists, Henno Martin and Hermann Korn, hid in this region for over two years to avoid internment, living off game and what they could find, and Martin later wrote a book about it, published in English as The Sheltered Desert. Their story is a reminder of how harsh and beautiful the place is. The Topnaar people, who have lived along the river for generations, harvest the !nara melon, a spiny plant that grows in the dunes and provides food and income.

Riding here means gravel and a lot of space. The road is usually in decent condition, but loose stones, washboard and sand drifts can catch you out, and the gradients into the canyon are steep enough to need care. Wind often blows hard in the afternoon, throwing dust across the road, and in the middle of summer the heat is intense. Watch for oryx and springbok that wander across the track, and give lorries plenty of space, as they raise clouds of dust.

Services are almost non-existent along this stretch. Solitaire, to the south-east, and Walvis Bay, on the coast, are the places for fuel and supplies, and it is sensible to carry extra fuel and plenty of water. If you stop in the canyon, be aware that flash floods are possible after rain in the distant highlands, even if the sky above you is clear, so do not camp in the riverbed. A pause on the rim, with the silence and the heat shimmering off the rocks, is a good reminder of the scale of this desert.
t.khorixas@-20.4,15.0:
Khorixas is not a place most people plan to see, but it is where the dry heart of Damaraland has its administrative office, a straggle of low buildings, shops and a petrol station on the gravel and tar roads of Kunene. The town, with about twelve thousand people, was laid out in the 1970s as the capital of the old Damaraland homeland, and while it lacks the charm of a colonial town, it serves a vast area and is a lively place, full of minibus taxis, market stalls and people who have come from distant farms to buy supplies.

Its importance for travellers is the sights close by. About sixty kilometres to the west lies Twyfelfontein, a valley of red sandstone with some of the largest concentrations of rock engravings in Africa, carved by hunter-gatherers thousands of years ago and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Closer to town, a petrified forest holds the remains of huge tree trunks, turned to stone about 280 million years ago, and swept here by floods before being buried. Nearby, the Burnt Mountain glows in the late sun, and the Organ Pipes, a cliff of dolerite columns, stand in a dry gorge.

On two wheels, the roads here are a mix of tar and gravel, running through open, dry country of scattered mopane and acacia, flat-topped hills and low ridges. The tar roads are long and straight, and gravel to the west toward Palmwag crosses dry riverbeds and stony plains, with opportunities to see desert-adapted wildlife such as oryx, springbok and, with luck, elephant and giraffe. Heat is strong, wind blows dust across the track, and rains in summer can cause flash floods. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times to ride.

As a regional centre, Khorixas has fuel stations, a bank with an ATM, supermarkets, and a few guesthouses and campsites, and it is the last dependable stop before the remote country to the west. Fill the tank, buy water and food, and carry spare supplies for the road ahead. The people are friendly, and a chat at a petrol station often yields useful news about road conditions. Plan to be off the road by dusk, because animals wander freely and visibility is poor.
t.waterberg namibia@-20.5,17.2:
The Waterberg is a wall of red sandstone that rises about two hundred metres out of the flat bushveld of central Namibia, running for roughly fifty kilometres. Its flat top, fed by springs that seep from the rock, supports woodland and wildlife unlike anything on the plains below, and the escarpment, in rust and gold, glows at sunrise and sunset. The plateau is a national park, home to rare species such as sable and roan antelope, white and black rhinos, and a colony of Cape vultures that nests on the cliffs.

It is also a place of heavy history. In August 1904, at the foot of the plateau, German colonial troops defeated a large Herero force in the Battle of Waterberg, and the survivors were driven into the Omaheke desert, where thousands died of thirst. A genocide followed, and the memory remains a painful part of Namibia's story. A small cemetery near the rest camp holds the graves of German soldiers, and Herero people still come to the area to remember. It is a place to be quiet and respectful, and local guides tell the story with dignity.

The ride in takes you across a landscape of thorn scrub and cattle farms, where the straight road to the escarpment is lined by fences and acacia trees, and the plateau appears on the horizon like a ship. The final approach is on gravel or tar, depending on the route, and livestock and wildlife wander across, so keep your speed moderate. Heat in summer is intense, and the rains bring afternoon thunderstorms, so mornings are better. Winter nights are cold but the days are bright, and the dry season is the best time for wildlife.

Okakarara, about twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with a population of about five thousand and basic fuel and supplies, while Otjiwarongo, farther on, has a wider range of services. Fill the tank before you reach the plateau and carry water. The rest camp offers accommodation, a restaurant and a pool, and a short walk leads to a viewpoint above the plains. Take binoculars, wear a hat, and be sure to book ahead in the holiday season.
t.spreetshoogte pass point 1@-23.9,16.0:
Solitaire is hardly a place at all, which is exactly why riders remember it. A petrol station, a general store, a small campsite, a scatter of rusted car wrecks half buried in sand and a bakery whose apple pie is spoken of from Windhoek to Walvis Bay: that is the whole settlement, planted on the gravel plains where the Namib meets the foot of the escarpment. Everything around it is space, pale grass, red dunes in the west and the long blue line of the mountains in the east.

The fuel is the reason many people turn off the road. This is one of the few reliable pumps in a very large stretch of country, with Sesriem and the Sossusvlei dunes to the south-west and the Kuiseb canyon to the north, and the sensible habit is to top up every time you pass. Fill the tank and any spare can, buy water, and then, because you are a human being, eat a slice of the pie. The bakery was started by a man known as Moose, who has become something of a local legend among overlanders.

The riding here is gravel, and the roads around Solitaire are graded but unsurfaced. The C14 and C19 run through open plains where the surface can be hard and fast or soft and corrugated, depending on grading and recent traffic. Wind is constant, and sand drifts across the track, so keep your speed measured and your eyes well ahead. Afternoon heat can be severe, so start early and plan your stops. Night riding is not wise, because oryx, springbok and the occasional zebra wander near the road.

The landscape is old and strange. The Namib is thought to be the oldest desert in the world, and the mountains to the east are part of the Great Escarpment that runs along the coast of southern Africa. From here the Spreetshoogte Pass climbs onto the highlands, one of the steepest and most dramatic roads in Namibia, and riders who know the country treat Solitaire as the place to prepare for it.

Water, shade and a chance to check tyre pressures and luggage straps are what Solitaire offers, and they are worth more than they sound. Carry cash, because card machines are not always working, and be ready for dust, which finds its way into everything. Evenings here are beautiful, with the sunset turning the mountains red and the stars coming out in a sky of quite extraordinary depth.
t.spreetshoogte pass point 2@-23.7,16.2:
Northeast of Solitaire the road starts its argument with the escarpment. The Spreetshoogte Pass is a gravel track that climbs from the Namib plains to the highlands of the Khomas Hochland, and it is famous for its gradient. Locals describe it as one of the steepest passes in Namibia, and the engineers who built it were not bashful about taking the shortest line up the hill.

The riding demands real attention. The surface is graded gravel with loose stones, sections of corrugation and steep concrete or hard-packed strips on the sharpest ramps. Low gears and steady throttle are the way to climb, and engine braking is essential on the descent, as the front brake can lock on loose ground. If you meet a vehicle coming the other way, the narrow sections can be tight, so hold your line and let the heavier machine pass. Do not try the pass in rain, because the surface can become slick, and avoid it in the heat of midday, when the engine and the rider are both under strain.

The geology is plain to see. Layers of rock, tilted and worn, form the face of the escarpment, with dry watercourses cutting through it. The vegetation shifts as you climb, from sparse desert grass on the plain to shrubs and hardy trees on the slopes, and the air becomes cooler and a little less dry. The views back toward the Namib are huge, with the red dunes and gravel plains laid out like a map under a hazy sky.

Wildlife can be seen if you are quiet and lucky. Baboons live on the rocky slopes, and kudu, oryx and mountain zebra are found on the plateau. Eagles and vultures circle on the thermals. The pass is a reminder that the desert is not empty, but a place where life has adapted to heat, drought and wind.

Carry water, since the climb is thirsty work and help is distant, and tell someone your plan. Mobile signal is patchy or absent, so a basic repair kit and tyre pump are worth carrying. Take your time, enjoy the view at the top, and be ready for a strong wind at the crest.
t.spreetshoogte pass point 3@-23.6,16.3:
Up on the rim, the world changes shape. The highlands above the Spreetshoogte Pass are cool, open and surprisingly green after the Namib, a high plateau of grass and thorn scrub that rolls away toward Windhoek. Cattle and game farms spread across it, separated by long fences and gravel roads, and the light has a clean, thin quality that is easy to love after the heat of the desert.

For a rider, the plateau means faster gravel and the chance to relax after the pass. The roads are graded, usually in decent condition, though corrugations and loose patches appear without warning. The wide-open views make distances hard to judge, and it is easy to underestimate how long a section will take. Cattle grids and sudden dips in the road are common, and a sandy patch can appear at the bottom of a dry riverbed. Keep your speed reasonable, especially when carrying luggage, and avoid riding at dusk, when wildlife is most active.

The Khomas Hochland takes its name from the Khoekhoe word for the area and the German word for highland, and the mix of languages reflects the history of the region. Farms here were established by German settlers in the colonial era, and some still carry names from that period. Before them, the land belonged to Herero and Nama peoples, and earlier still to San hunters, and traces of all three can be found in place names and rock shelters.

The ridge behind you is part of the Great Escarpment, and the contrast between the highland and the coastal plain is dramatic. Looking back west from the top, you can see the pass dropping away and the plains of the Namib stretching into haze. A cool breeze often blows here, and the nights are cold even in summer, so a warm layer is useful.

Services are almost nonexistent on this part of the route. Farms may offer accommodation, and some have campsites, but fuel is not sold on the road, and Solitaire or Windhoek are the places to refill. Carry water, spare fuel if your range is short, and enough food for a day. A satellite messenger or a plan to check in with someone is a wise precaution, because a breakdown here could mean a long wait.
t.sossusvlei desert route point 1@-24.5,15:
Everything about the approach teaches you scale. The plains run out toward a horizon that looks too far away, mountains stand like cut-outs on the east side, and the road from the main gravel arteries delivers you here with a steady rumble of corrugation.

The name is older than any lodge. Sesriem means 'six belts' in Afrikaans, and the story goes that early settlers had to knot six lengths of oryx hide together to lower a bucket into the narrow gorge of the Tsauchab River to reach water. That gorge still exists, a short walk from the gate, a slot a few dozen metres deep, cut through conglomerate and cool in the shade. After rain the Tsauchab can flow a long way toward the sand sea, but in most years it never gets there, which is why the vleis downstream stay dry.

The tar road that leads from Sesriem deep into the dune sea is the reason the route exists. It runs for around sixty kilometres between red ridges that grow taller as you go, and the gate is the control on when you can use it, because the park gates follow sunrise and sunset rather than the clock on your wrist. Be at the gate early. Dawn colours the dunes, the temperature is kind, and the oryx and springbok walk the road verges before the heat sends them into the shade. By late morning the sand radiates and the road shimmers.

It helps to remember that Sesriem is a small cluster of campsite and lodging rather than a town, so food, water and anything you forgot are handled in the little complex here, and larger supplies come from the bigger settlements to the north and east. The sky here is among the darkest on any ride in the country, so an evening spent at a camp with a thermos and nothing but stars overhead is as good as the riding.

Wind is the thing to respect in the Namib. It can shift sand across the tar in a few hours, and a rider coming around a bend on a dune-crested stretch should expect a thin carpet of grit.
t.sossusvlei desert route point 2@-24.7,15:
Most people know this stretch by one number. Dune 45 is named for its distance from the park gate at Sesriem, forty-five kilometres, and it is about as far as many visitors go on a first morning, which means it is climbed, photographed and trampled long before the heat arrives.

The Namib sand sea is among the oldest living deserts on Earth, and the dunes are red because of iron oxide that coats each grain and darkens with age and exposure. The oldest, deepest-coloured dunes are the ones furthest from the coast. They are shaped by winds that blow in different directions through the seasons, which is why the crests are so sharp and the star dunes have several arms. A rider who has only seen sand in pictures is usually struck by how silent it is, and by the way a single footprint can survive for hours.

The riding is almost an afterthought, but it is a very good afterthought. The tarmac is smooth, wide and nearly empty before nine o'clock, with long curves that follow the flats between ridges. The corners are gentle, but sand can drift across them, and the sun low in your eyes at dawn makes it hard to see the thin tongues of it. Keep your speed honest, stay off the soft verge, and expect the occasional oryx at the edge of the road.

If you plan to climb the dune, leave the bike on firm ground and go barefoot or in light shoes, because riding boots fill with sand immediately and the last part of the ridge is a slow, comic staircase. The walk takes the better part of half an hour and the view from the top is of a corrugated red world running in lines to a horizon of heat haze.

Water, hat and sun protection matter more than anything else here. There is no shade at all, and the sun at midday can turn a casual stop into something you regret. Shortly after sunrise is the sweet hour.
t.sossusvlei desert route point 3@-24.7,15:
Past the main dune run, the tarmac ends and the desert takes over, which is the point where this route becomes more of a pilgrimage than a ride. The surface under your wheels shifts from asphalt to sand within a few hundred metres, and the standard advice is that anything without four-wheel drive stops at the car park and walks.

The word vlei is Afrikaans for a shallow pan or marsh, and Sossusvlei, which is usually explained as 'the place of no return', refers to the way water flows in and goes nowhere. It evaporates, or sinks. When a good rainy season sends the Tsauchab down in flood, the pans fill with a thin sheet of water and the dunes mirror themselves in it, and then the water is gone within weeks, leaving a pale clay floor cracked into plates.

The dunes here are called star dunes because they have several arms that radiate from a high central crest, each one shaped by winds from different directions. Some of the tallest in the Namib rise more than three hundred metres above the pan, and the colour changes through the day from soft apricot at dawn to a hard burnt red at noon and a violet shade at dusk. The only constant is silence, broken by wind and the odd gecko or darkling beetle leaving tracks.

This is a spot where the right attitude is patience. Take your time, drink water often, and treat any desire to ride on the sand with suspicion, because a bike that goes down in deep sand in this heat is a long and exhausting job to lift. Park on firm ground, walk the final stretch and carry your helmet and gloves; the shuttle vehicles that run the sand section exist for good reason.

Dawn is the best light by a wide margin, and by ten the sun overhead flattens the colour and sends the temperature past comfortable. Plan the day backward from the gate time.
t.sossusvlei desert route point 4@-24.8,15:
Of all the places in this part of the Namib, Deadvlei is the one that turns up on postcards, and the reason is simple: it looks wrong in the best way. A white clay pan, baked hard, sits between walls of orange dune, and from its surface stand black, skeletal camelthorn trees, long dead, still upright.

The explanation is a story of water. The Tsauchab once flooded this hollow often enough for camelthorn trees to take root along it. Then the climate dried and dunes migrated across the river's route, cutting off the flow. The trees died where they stood, and the desert air was so dry that the wood never rotted. Estimates of how long ago that happened, and how old the trees are, vary, but figures of several centuries up to nearly a thousand years are the ones usually quoted, and what you see is blackened by sun rather than burnt.

Getting here is a day's work. The tar road from Sesriem runs a long way into the dunes and stops, the final few kilometres are deep sand, and the usual approach is on foot or by the shuttle. A rider on a standard bike leaves the machine at the end of the tarmac, so the real exercise in this place is the walk. It is not far, but sand pulls at each step, and the heat makes distance deceptive. Wear light, breathable clothing, and take more water than you expect to drink.

Photographers know the trick: arrive at the first light, when the shadow line cuts a sharp diagonal across the pan and one side of the big dune is glowing while the other is still dark. After that the sun comes up quickly and the whole bowl turns into a reflector. By the middle of the day the crowds and the heat arrive together.

Walk quietly if you can. Besides the odd tourist, you may notice small tracks of beetles and lizards crossing the clay, and the occasional oryx on the dune slopes. Few places make desert life feel so improbable, and so stubbornly alive.
t.near catania@37.5,15.1:
Catania has been knocked down and rebuilt so many times that it has made a style out of resilience. Lava from Etna overran parts of the city in 1669, and then in 1693 a devastating earthquake flattened it almost entirely. The rebuilding produced one of the most striking Baroque cities in Italy, built with dark grey lava stone set off against pale limestone, with wide straight streets designed to offer escape routes in future disasters. The centre is part of the Late Baroque Towns of the Val di Noto World Heritage Site, and Etna looms over everything, often smoking at the end of the Via Etnea.

In the Piazza del Duomo stands the city's symbol, a lava-stone elephant carrying an Egyptian obelisk, known affectionately as u Liotru. The cathedral holds the relics of Saint Agatha, the patron saint, whose festival in early February brings huge crowds onto the streets for days. The composer Vincenzo Bellini was born here, and his name graces the opera house, a park and a pastry or two. The fish market, la Pescheria, behind the cathedral, is a riot of noise, colour and swordfish heads every morning except Sunday.

Riding in Catania itself is an exercise in assertiveness: traffic is chaotic, scooters weave in every gap, the cobbles are slippery when wet and parking is creative. But the city is a gateway to some of the best riding in Sicily. The roads up Etna, from Nicolosi to the Rifugio Sapienza or around the north side through Linguaglossa, are superb, and south towards Siracusa and the Baroque towns of Noto, Modica and Ragusa, the Iblei hills offer twisting roads and wonderful views.

Petrol, tyres and mechanics are easy to find in a city this size, and the food alone justifies an overnight stop. Locals will argue that the fried rice ball here is the masculine arancino rather than the Palermo arancina; pasta alla Norma, with aubergine and salted ricotta, is named after Bellini's opera; and summer breakfast means almond or pistachio granita with a soft brioche to dip. Keep valuables off the bike, use a guarded garage overnight, and be ready for the volcano to dust everything, including your visor, with fine black grit after an eruption.
t.near nicolosi@37.7,15.0:
Nicolosi is the town where Etna starts to feel real. It sits on the southern slope of the volcano at around seven hundred metres, a place of low houses built from black lava stone, steep streets and a surprising number of cafes, and it is the usual gateway for anyone heading up the mountain. Above it, the dark cones of Monti Rossi, formed in the eruption of 1669, look like two big red-brown humps against the sky. That eruption was one of the most destructive in the volcano's history, and its lava flowed down the slopes and reached the walls of Catania, leaving a landscape that still looks raw.

Etna is the tallest active volcano in Europe, at a little over three thousand three hundred metres, though the exact height changes with each eruption, and the whole mountain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The soil from its ash is fertile, and on the lower slopes you find vineyards, pistachio and citrus orchards, and fields of prickly pear. The wine made here is highly regarded, and a glass of local red with a plate of pasta is a good reward after a day on the bike.

For riders, Nicolosi is the base and the starting line. The road from here to Rifugio Sapienza, the provincial road that climbs the south flank, is wide and well surfaced, with a series of bends through lava fields and pine woods. The gradient is steady, and the views of the sea and Catania open behind you as you climb. Be careful of ash and grit on the surface after eruptions, and of cold, fast-changing weather higher up. Traffic can be heavy at weekends and in summer, when buses and tour groups go up and down.

The town has everything you might need, from fuel to supermarkets, pharmacies and restaurants. Fill the tank here before the climb, as there is nothing above except the souvenir shops and cafes around the refuge. There are good bakeries too, and the Sicilian morning ritual of a brioche stuffed with granita is worth trying. Catania, about twenty kilometres south, is the nearest large city with an airport and plenty of services.

Nicolosi also has the Etna park office, where you can find maps and information on the trails, the cable car and local guides. Check conditions before going up, because the authorities close access to the upper slopes when the volcano is active, and it is worth listening to what they say.
